cues.text: Let's turn now to quality of service, usually shortened to QoS, and the mechanisms and models behind it.
Start with what QoS actually is.
Quality of Service manages the relative treatment of different kinds of traffic when they contend for the same resources.
The key word is relative.
When a link is not congested, every packet gets through and there is little to manage.
QoS matters when demand exceeds capacity, and it decides which traffic is served first, which waits, and which is dropped.
There are several models for doing this.
The first is best effort.
Best effort makes no specific guarantee at all.
Packets are forwarded as well as the network can manage, with no promise about delay, loss or throughput.
The second model is IntServ, short for Integrated Services, used together with RSVP, the Resource Reservation Protocol.
IntServ with RSVP reserves resources for each individual flow.

But strict guarantees only hold if every device along the path supports the mechanism, and admission control is applied along that path, meaning a device can refuse a new reservation when it cannot honour it.
There is also a cost.
Because every flow needs its own state kept in the devices, per-flow state limits how far this model can scale.
The third model is DiffServ, short for Differentiated Services.
Instead of tracking each flow, DiffServ classifies and marks traffic into aggregates, which are groups of traffic that receive the same treatment.
Routers then apply per-hop behaviours, meaning each router decides how to treat a packet based on its marking, hop by hop.
Because it avoids per-flow state, DiffServ scales better for the diverse traffic found in enterprise networks.
Two further points.
MPLS traffic engineering, where MPLS means Multiprotocol Label Switching, may support control over the path that traffic takes.
And remember this firmly: QoS does not create bandwidth.
It only decides how the available bandwidth is shared.
Now let's look at classification and marking.
Classification identifies traffic.
It can do so using trusted headers, using applications, or using policies.
Marking then records the result on the packet or frame.
At Layer 3, marking sets the DSCP, the Differentiated Services Code Point, which is 6 bits in the IP differentiated-services field.
At Layer 2, marking uses 802.1p PCP, the Priority Code Point, which is 3 bits.
Several common DSCP values are worth knowing.
EF, Expedited Forwarding, uses DSCP 46, and it commonly marks real-time voice carried in RTP, the Real-time Transport Protocol.
AF, Assured Forwarding, provides classes and also drop precedences, so within a class some traffic can be dropped before other traffic.
CS markings are the Class Selector values, and CS3 is often used for signalling, within a defined policy.
Finally, DF, the default, is DSCP 0, and that means best effort.
There is an important security and design caution here.
Do not trust every endpoint's self-marking.
A device could mark its own traffic as high priority whether or not it deserves it.
So establish a trust boundary, and remark traffic as needed when it crosses that boundary.
Next, queuing, and related congestion tools.
FIFO, first in first out, serves packets in arrival order.
Strict priority serves the highest priority traffic first, but if it is unlimited it can starve other traffic, so lower classes may get little or nothing.
Weighted fair queuing and class-based queues share the capacity among classes according to weights or allocations.
A low-latency queue gives bounded priority to real-time traffic, so the traffic is served quickly but the priority is limited.
Then we have two different rate controls.
Shaping buffers and delays traffic in order to smooth its rate.
Policing enforces a rate by dropping excess traffic or remarking it.
So shaping delays, while policing drops or remarks.
For congestion management there is WRED, Weighted Random Early Detection, which can probabilistically drop packets earlier, before queues are full, to manage congestion.
And ECN, Explicit Congestion Notification, may signal congestion where it is supported.
Finally, admission control and capacity planning protect priority traffic, because no queuing scheme can rescue a link that has been promised more than it can carry.
Let's put numbers on this with an example.
Suppose there are 20 simultaneous VoIP calls, with an estimated 100 kilobits per second per call, including overhead.
That requires about 2 megabits per second in each direction.
You should reserve appropriate headroom beyond that, rate-limit the priority class, and allocate minimum shares to business traffic and to bulk traffic, so they are not starved.
You should also verify the actual codec, the packetization, and the tunnel overhead, because the 100 kilobits per second figure is only an estimate.
Remember the arithmetic limit too.
A 10 megabit per second link cannot serve 12 megabits per second of guaranteed commitments simultaneously.
Guarantees cannot add up to more than the link.
The practical sequence is this.
Mark voice at ingress, preserve the DSCP across managed hops, configure egress queues, and test under load.
Finally, a conceptual workflow on Huawei VRP, the Versatile Routing Platform.
This is conceptual, and the exact syntax is model-specific.
First, define a traffic classifier that matches voice DSCP or an ACL, an access control list.
Second, define a traffic behavior, with marking, queueing or policing as supported.
Third, define a traffic policy that binds the classifier to the behavior.
Fourth, apply that policy on the relevant interface and in the relevant direction.
Fifth, inspect the counters.
Two cautions apply.
Do not paste one vendor's syntax into another vendor's equipment.
And do not promise enforcement without interface support.
